title: Quantum statistical enhancement of collective behaviour in a bosonic active Ising model
authors: Kian L. Assent, Emil Strauch, Sabine H. L. Klapp, André Eckardt, Alexander Schnell
abstract: Collective behaviour such as flocking (the collective motion of a spontaneously formed group along a common direction) or aster formation (the binding of opposing flocks, inhibiting each others motion) are intriguing emergent phenomena in active systems with local alignment rules. Until recently, their occurrence was mainly studied for classical systems, a prime example being the active Ising model (AIM), which translates the main ingredients of flocking and aster formation (i.e., alignment and self-propulsion) to a lattice framework. Here we introduce and study a one-dimensional (1D) quantum lattice variant of the AIM, based on ideal bosons with a spin degree of freedom. We find that both the collective behaviours of the 1D classical model, flocking and aster formation, are markedly enhanced by the bosonic quantum statistics. This contrasts with a recent quantum generalization of the AIM based onto hard-core bosons [Khasseh et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 248302 (2025)], where flocking, but neither its quantum-statistical stabilization nor aster states were observed as a consequence of interactions. Moreover, we investigate the competition of this quantum statistical stabilization of collective phases with their suppression by the quantum fluctuations induced by a transverse external magnetic field.
summary: This paper analyzes a bosonic active Ising model to study emergent collective behaviors like flocking and aster formation in non-equilibrium settings. The key finding is that bosonic quantum statistics significantly enhance the stability of these ordered phases compared to classical models. Using mean-field theory, the authors map out phase diagrams showing how this enhancement competes with suppression from external magnetic fields.
main_problem: The study investigates how bosonic quantum statistics enhance collective behaviors like flocking and aster formation in an active Ising model, contrasting these findings with classical models and other quantum generalizations.
main_result: Bosonic indistinguishability markedly enhances the stability of both flocking and aster phases compared to classical predictions, allowing these ordered states to persist at higher temperatures. Furthermore, the analysis maps out how external transverse magnetic fields suppress these collective phenomena.
method: The authors employ a mean-field approximation on the Lindblad master equation for ideal bosons, deriving closed kinetic equations for single-particle density matrices and mean occupations.
model_or_system: The system is a one-dimensional quantum lattice variant of the Active Ising Model (AIM) based on ideal bosons with spin degrees of freedom ($\uparrow$ and $\downarrow$). The dynamics are governed by a Lindblad master equation incorporating coherent, spin-flip, and biased hopping processes.
key_observables: Mean magnetization ($\langle m angle$), local magnetizations ($ho_l, ho_{l+1}$), mean occupations ($\langle n_{ls} angle$), and the critical temperature for phase transitions.
important_parameters: Activity parameter ($\epsilon$), inverse temperature ($ eta=1/T$), external transverse magnetic field strength ($\omega$), and system density ($ho_0$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies heavily on mean-field approximations and the use of Wick's theorem to truncate the BBGKY hierarchy, neglecting higher-order correlations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate phase diagrams comparing classical vs. quantum predictions (showing enhanced stability in the quantum case), and dynamic simulations showing the formation and evolution of large moving flocks or stationary asters under different parameter regimes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the full quantum master equation to deriving mean-field kinetic equations for occupations, analyzing the classical limit recovery, quantifying bosonic enhancement effects, and finally mapping out phase diagrams dependent on temperature, density, and external fields.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete theoretical framework for understanding non-equilibrium collective dynamics in quantum many-body systems. The explicit demonstration of 'bosonic enhancement' offers insights into how quantum statistics can stabilize complex ordered phases beyond classical mean-field predictions, which is highly relevant to AMO physics and quantum simulation.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: (a) The particle’s spin species governs its pre- ferred direction of movement. (b) The lattice sites of the AIM are initially occupied by a random distribution of particles. (c) Large groups of same-species particles mov- ing around the AIM are considered a flock, while (d) a large group of opposite-species-particles remaining dor- mant on neighboring sites are called an aster.

FIG. 2: Phase diagram of the classical active Ising model, Eq. (4), (a) in the T −D plane (for ε = 0.7, γ = 1, ρ0 = 10 and L = 100) and (b) in the T −ρ0 plane for D = 1 (other parameters as in (a)). Yellow dots indicate the formation of asters (according to the critierion given the main text). The results are consistent with [44].

FIG. 3: Different setups of the AIM under investigation and the corresponding master equations. In the classical limit, all quantum effects are neglected when evaluat- ing the expectation values. When focusing on dissipative quantum effects, the coherences resulting from a sepa- ration of ⟨n · n′⟩are set to zero. Lastly, to simulate an external influence, in our case a magnetic field, the sys- tem is exposed to an external Hamiltonian H( ⃗B) ̸= 0. The resulting dynamics include quantum coherences.

FIG. 4: Dynamics of the mean-field kinetic equations of the AIM with classical particles (L = 1000, N = 10000, D = 1 and ε = 0.7) developing (a) asters at T = 0.35 as well as (c) flocks at T = 0.45. (b),(d) Spin densities and magnetization along vertical cuts through (a) and (c), respectively, at a late time [indicated by vertical dashed lines in (a) and (c)]. In (b) we zoom into a few sites, to resolve the shape of an aster.

FIG. 5: Dynamics of a large quantum AIM of ideal bosons (L = 1000, N = 10000 and ε = 0.7) developing (a) asters at D = 0.2 and T = 10 as well as (c) flocks at D = 3, T = 10. (b),(d) Absolute magnetization of each lattice site at a late time of figures (a) and (c), respectively [indicated by vertical dashed lines in (a) and (c)]. The aster phase evolves differently when compared to the classical model, with multiple neighbouring peaks of opposite magnetization. Additionally, the flock appears sharply localized at its edge instead of the continuous curve found in Fig. 4.
